# Introduction

Environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys often measure DNA with quantitative PCR (qPCR).
The response is the cycle threshold (Ct), the PCR cycle at which amplification is detected: lower Ct values mean more DNA, and some reactions never amplify.
Converting Ct to DNA concentration needs a *standard curve*, estimated from laboratory reactions of known concentration ("standards") run on the same PCR plates as the field samples.

The `stdcurve()` family fits the standard curves and the spatial model together, so uncertainty in the curves carries through to the estimates of DNA concentration.
This follows the approach of @liu2026eulachon, who mapped the marine distribution of eulachon (*Thaleichthys pacificus*) in the Northeast Pacific from eDNA with a joint model of qPCR standards and spatiotemporal DNA concentration.
The model uses two data sets:

1. the field samples (passed to `data`, as in any sdmTMB model), with a Ct response and a `plate` column, and
2. the laboratory standards (passed to `stdcurve(standards = )`), with columns `plate`, `ct`, and `concentration`.

See the [model description](https://sdmTMB.github.io/sdmTMB/articles/model-description.html) for the equations.
In brief, the linear predictor is log DNA concentration (the family has a log link), and each plate has four coefficients---an intercept and slope for positive Ct values (Gaussian), and an intercept and slope for the probability of detection (logistic)---that are random effects across plates.

# Simulating data

We'll simulate standards for 20 plates, with 3 replicates at each of 7 concentrations.

```{r sim-standards}
set.seed(123)
n_plates <- 20
plates <- paste0("plate", seq_len(n_plates))

# plate coefficients: Ct intercept, Ct slope, detection intercept and slope
mu <- c(38, -1.45, -1, 0.5)
sigma <- c(0.6, 0.05, 0.3, 0.1)
xi <- sapply(1:4, function(k) rnorm(n_plates, mu[k], sigma[k]))
phi <- 0.3 # SD of positive Ct values

# Ct values for log concentration `x` on plates `j`
sim_ct <- function(x, j) {
  p <- plogis(xi[j, 3] + xi[j, 4] * exp(x)) # detection on concentration
  rbinom(length(x), 1, p) * rnorm(length(x), xi[j, 1] + xi[j, 2] * x, phi)
}

standards <- expand.grid(
  concentration = 10^seq(-1, 5),
  replicate = 1:3,
  plate = plates,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
standards$ct <- sim_ct(log(standards$concentration), match(standards$plate, plates))
head(standards)
```

Non-detections in the standards can be coded as `0` or `NA`.

Next, the field samples: a spatial field of log DNA concentration observed at 500 locations, each sample analyzed on one of the plates.

```{r sim-samples}
predictor_dat <- data.frame(X = runif(500), Y = runif(500))
mesh <- make_mesh(predictor_dat, c("X", "Y"), cutoff = 0.08)
samples <- sdmTMB_simulate(
  formula = ~ 1,
  data = predictor_dat,
  mesh = mesh,
  family = gaussian(),
  range = 0.5,
  sigma_O = 0.5,
  phi = 0.01,
  B = 1, # mean log concentration
  seed = 123
)
samples$plate <- sample(plates, nrow(samples), replace = TRUE)
samples$ct <- sim_ct(samples$eta, match(samples$plate, plates))
mean(samples$ct == 0) # proportion of non-detections
```

In `data`, non-detections must be `0`; `NA` is treated as a missing observation.

# Fitting

```{r fit, message=TRUE}
fit <- sdmTMB(
  ct ~ 1,
  data = samples,
  mesh = mesh,
  family = stdcurve(standards = standards)
)
fit
sanity(fit)
```

Here, `sanity()` flags the standard deviations of the plate coefficients (`ln_std_sigma`).
Variation among plates in the detection curve is often weakly identified, and its estimate can collapse toward zero, as the detection intercept SD does here:

```{r sd-hyper}
get_stdcurve(fit)$hyper
```

If so, that standard deviation can be fixed at a small value with `map` and `start` (the order is Ct intercept, Ct slope, detection intercept, detection slope):

```{r map-sd, message=TRUE}
fit <- update(fit, control = sdmTMBcontrol(
  map = list(ln_std_sigma = factor(c(1, 2, NA, 3))),
  start = list(ln_std_sigma = c(0, -2, log(0.01), -2))
))
sanity(fit)
```

The intercept is the mean log DNA concentration (simulated as 1):

```{r tidy}
tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
tidy(fit, effects = "ran_pars", conf.int = TRUE)
```

The `phi` parameter is the standard deviation of positive Ct values.

# Standard curves

`get_stdcurve()` returns the plate coefficients and their hyperparameters (the means and standard deviations across plates):

```{r get-stdcurve}
sc <- get_stdcurve(fit)
sc$hyper
head(sc$plates)
```

The estimated plate curves are close to the simulated ones:

```{r plot-plates}
true <- data.frame(
  plate = rep(plates, 4),
  term = rep(c("ct_intercept", "ct_slope", "det_intercept", "det_slope"), each = n_plates),
  true = c(xi)
)
d <- merge(sc$plates, true)
ggplot(d, aes(true, estimate)) +
  geom_abline() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = estimate - 2 * std.error, ymax = estimate + 2 * std.error)) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free")
```

Positive Ct values on plate $j$ have mean `ct_intercept + ct_slope * log(concentration)`, so we can draw each plate's fitted curve through its standards:

```{r plot-standards}
# long to wide: a plates x coefficients matrix (one estimate per cell)
est <- xtabs(estimate ~ plate + term, data = sc$plates)
j <- standards$plate
standards$ct_hat <- est[j, "ct_intercept"] + est[j, "ct_slope"] * log(standards$concentration)
ggplot(standards, aes(log(concentration))) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ifelse(is.na(ct) | ct == 0, NA, ct)), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ct_hat, group = plate), alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(y = "Ct", x = "log concentration (copies/µl)")
```

# Predictions

Predictions don't need a plate. By default they are on the link scale, log DNA concentration:

```{r predict}
p <- predict(fit)
ggplot(p, aes(eta, est)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline() +
  labs(x = "Simulated log concentration", y = "Estimated log concentration")
```

A prediction grid works as with any other family:

```{r predict-grid}
grid <- expand.grid(X = seq(0, 1, length.out = 50), Y = seq(0, 1, length.out = 50))
pg <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)
ggplot(pg, aes(X, Y, fill = est)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "log conc.")
```

Because the family has a log link, `type = "response"` gives DNA concentration, and derived quantities such as `get_index()` are of concentration (here, summed over the grid cells, each with area 1):

```{r index}
head(predict(fit, newdata = grid, type = "response"))
get_index(fit, newdata = grid, area = 1)
```

# Residuals and simulation

Randomized quantile residuals treat the model as a hurdle: a non-detection is placed uniformly in the probability of non-detection, and a positive Ct by its Gaussian distribution.

```{r residuals}
samples$resid <- residuals(fit, type = "mle-eb")
qqnorm(samples$resid)
qqline(samples$resid)
```

`simulate()` draws new Ct values from the fitted model (conditional on the estimated plate curves):

```{r simulate}
s <- simulate(fit, nsim = 100)
c(observed = mean(samples$ct > 0), simulated = mean(s > 0))
```

# Other options

- `stdcurve(detection = "log_concentration")` models detection probability as linear in log concentration instead of concentration.
- Other column names (e.g., `Ct` from a lab export) can be given with the `plate`, `ct`, and `concentration` arguments of `stdcurve()`.
- Any of the usual sdmTMB model components (covariates, smoothers, spatiotemporal fields, offsets for, e.g., volume filtered) can be added to the model of log concentration.
